I have a pretty concrete concept/approach proposal for a "muxed e-test" that'd work with a slightly fancier multimeter than the COB bond test jig already in use, and would utilize a dense analog switch (transmission gate) based bus to connect a variety (think 200 on a full slot) of DUTs in 4-wire like "kelvin" connectivity to external pins to have separate sense and drive wires for all the contact/via/"pin" zones of the DUTs; to be used with e.g. Xyce predictor based selection of what operating points to measure under DC or near-DC conditions, in order to fine-tune the SPICE model of e.g. an SCL and use the 1000 such dies via their cheap COB bonding and a simple test jig (just needs decent volt/current meters behind for good measurements) to get statistically significant data on mismatch across similar structures right besides one another, across reticles on a wafer, and across wafers of a lot.

I'd think it could be scripted with librelane I just don't have the time to do that myself; in lieau of that it could be scripted with klayout (or magic) as it's essentially just a bus with switches underneath DUTs on one side and a digital decoder logic on the other side that just allows for externally selecting which DUT to mux to the bus. Just a decoder into one-hot select bits across the DUT slots should suffice.

DUTs would be SCL cells of sufficient notability, and a bunch of primitives that are lacking foundry open-source e-test coverage (e.g. there's no data on vias/contacts, there's no coverage for thin oxide native nmos at all, there's no coverage for (admittedly kinda DRC-breaking though IMO that's ERC domain and should be waived for at least test structures if modeling is good enough) short channel native NMOS, a LOT of devices lack mismatch characterization (e.g. shottkey diodes are just a start)).
No dynamic behavior intended.
I would like some latchup-type structures if they can be wired to be provoked into latchup with that analog mux, to get at least a hint of e-test coverage for such behavior as it ma not be catastrophic if the chip is prevented from melting itself via teh ensuing power dissipation.
Doesn't have to be _that_ fab SCL.
Can literally be an OSU IHP library for all it matters

For clarification I can guide someone who can write code well enough to read the docs and figure out how to do that scripting; they don't have to understand how the structures work but they should understand enough of ASIC design to grasp how the routing decisions for such matrix/bus structures can be drawn for density and still having reasonably decent signal quality. Don't want the modeling of the matrix to dominate the measurement uncertainty and 1/f noise modeling....

@Martin Schoeberl Let me address your two issues.

1. Nix is recompiling the binaries

This should not happen if you have the FOSSi Nix cache set up. Please follow the installation instructions at https://librelane.readthedocs.io/en/stable/installation/nix_installation/index.html, making sure you set up https://nix-cache.fossi-foundation.org as an additional Nix cache.

You can verify that the Nix cache has been set up correctly by starting a Nix shell with LibreLane (nothing should recompile):

```
$ nix shell github:librelane/librelane
$ librelane --smoke-test
```

2. ghdl-bin is not available for aarch64-linux

The ghdl-bin package (the VHDL simulator) is only available for x86_64-linux and aarch64-darwin. That is unfortunately a limitation of GHDL as it only targets these platforms afaik: https://github.com/ghdl/ghdl/releases/tag/v6.0.0

ghdl-bin is required by wafer.space because the Nix flake in the gf180mcu-project-template includes cocotb, and cocotb requires ghdl-bin during the check phase.

We can try to workaround this problem: You can simply remove the cocotb package from the Nix flake: https://github.com/wafer-space/gf180mcu-project-template/blob/0de7e394337a1f7f5303ac7a3681bf2481b58176/flake.nix#L71

This should allow you to enable the Nix shell and run LibreLane. However, you won't be able to run any simulations with cocotb.

Another workaround would be to disable the check phase in cocotb and remove ghdl-bin when the platform is aarch64-linux. Of course, then we can't be sure that cocotb will work as expected, but it will probably be fine. Let me know if you would like to give this a try.

Hi @Leo Moser (mole99) thank you for your detailed reply. As Tjark found a workaround for the Mac issue (Qt in KLayout has concurrency problems on MacOS) to set workers to 1, I am back being able to run native LibreLane for wafer.space on my Mac. I can drop my ARM Linux experiment. All set and looking forward to our first tapeout at wafer.space.
